summary: This is an April Fools' Day RFC. It proposes two joke ways of encoding Unicode characters, UTF-9 and UTF-18, aimed at systems with 9-bit bytes or 36-bit words, which are not much used today. It humorously contrasts with the real UTF-8.

eli5.summary: This is a joke. It suggests writing letters using odd-sized chunks, as if computers still worked that way, so that old machines could join in.

subtitle: Joke encoding formats for Unicode on 9-bit and 18-bit machines

tldr.problem: This is an April Fools' joke treating as if modern computer architectures still used 9-bit bytes (nonets) instead of the standard 8-bit bytes, claiming UTF-8 and UTF-16 are inefficient on such systems.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes UTF-9, which encodes Unicode characters in 9-bit nonets, and UTF-18, which uses pairs of nonets. The RFC includes conversion routines in PDP-10 assembly and C, written as if such systems were still in common use.
tldr.outcome: This is a humorous document. The 36-bit PDP-10 and other nonets-based architectures have been obsolete for decades. Modern systems use 8-bit bytes exclusively.

today: This is an April Fools' joke from 2005. No real support for UTF-9 or UTF-18 was ever implemented in IETF protocols, and the PDP-10 and other 36-bit architectures it targets have been obsolete for decades.

sections.title: The Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 4042 presents itself as a serious technical solution, claiming that some platforms (like the 36-bit PDP-10) use 9-bit nonets rather than 8-bit octets. The RFC argues that existing Unicode transformation formats like UTF-8 and UTF-16 waste bits on these systems. For example, UTF-8 can waste up to four bits per character when stored in nonets, and UTF-16 requires complex surrogate handling.

The humor lies in the premise: these architectures have been obsolete for decades, yet the RFC discusses them with complete technical seriousness, complete with assembly code in PDP-10 machine language.
sections.eli5: Imagine proposing a new way to write words just for computers that stopped being made before most people reading this were born.

sections.title: UTF-9 and UTF-18 Definitions
sections.content:
UTF-9 encodes Unicode codepoints using the low-order 8 bits of a 9-bit nonet, with the high-order bit indicating continuation. Basic Latin characters (U+0000 to U+00FF) fit in a single nonet, characters in the broader Basic Multilingual Plane (U+0100 to U+FFFF) require two nonets, and characters outside the BMP require three. UTF-18 uses pairs of nonets to form an 18-bit value, sufficient to represent most but not all of Unicode.

The RFC includes detailed examples showing how characters like Greek Alpha (U+0391) or Gothic letters (U+10330) would be encoded in octal notation, demonstrating the schemes work in principle.
sections.eli5: The proposal shows how you would split letters into these unusual-sized chunks, with examples of how various world letters would be broken up.

sections.title: Sample Routines and Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC includes conversion routines for both PDP-10 assembly language and C, demonstrating how to convert between Unicode codepoints (UCS-4) and UTF-9. The PDP-10 code includes mnemonics like TDZA (test and deposit), ILDB (increment and load byte), and POPJ (pop and jump), programming constructs specific to that obscure 1960s-era architecture.

The document notes that implementation experience shows UTF-9 and UTF-18 are 'quite simple' to implement on nonet-based architectures, but acknowledges that the IETF protocol suite is 'quite deficient' in supporting nonets for transport.
sections.eli5: The document includes actual code samples showing how you would write the conversion, treating these ancient computers as if they were still relevant for Internet standards work.
